analysis.one_liner: Bans new copper-nickel mining on federal land beside the Boundary Waters wilderness.
analysis.headline: A bill to block copper-nickel mining on 234,328 acres next to the Boundary Waters died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently bar new mineral claims and mining leases on about 234,328 acres of federal land and water in Minnesota's Rainy River Watershed, which drains directly into the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and Voyageurs National Park. It is aimed at sulfide-ore copper-nickel mining, which produces acid runoff that can leach metals into water. The bill leaves access to sand, gravel, granite, iron ore, and taconite in place.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the people who gain would be canoeists, campers, and anglers who use the Boundary Waters and Voyageurs National Park; the tourism and outfitting businesses of northeastern Minnesota, which the bill's own findings project would add 1,500 to 4,600 jobs and $100 million to $900 million in income over 20 years under a withdrawal; and the Ojibwe bands whose 1854 treaty hunting and fishing rights cover the area. The water itself is the biggest beneficiary: the watershed holds roughly 20 percent of the fresh water in the entire National Forest System, and the bill would remove the main threat of acid mine drainage to it.

how_it_helps.text: Withdraws approximately 234,328 acres of federal land and waters in the Rainy River Watershed from all mineral entry, claim staking, leasing, geothermal leasing, and disposal under public land and mining laws.

Protects the Boundary Waters and Voyageurs National Park from sulfide-ore copper mining pollution: when sulfide minerals are exposed to air and water they form sulfuric acid that leaches copper, lead, arsenic-family metals, and other contaminants into groundwater and lakes, and a cited peer-reviewed study found every one of 14 operating U.S. copper sulfide mines had spills or accidental releases.

Protects the region's tourism economy; the bill's findings state that a mineral withdrawal would produce 1,500 to 4,600 more jobs and $100 million to $900 million more income over 20 years than allowing the mining.
Protects the treaty resources of the Grand Portage, Fond du Lac, and Bois Forte bands of Ojibwe, whose 1854 Treaty of LaPointe hunting, fishing, and gathering rights cover the area.

Leaves everyday uses intact: the Forest Service may still permit removal of sand, gravel, granite, iron ore, and taconite from the withdrawn area as long as it does not harm the watershed's water, air, or forest habitat.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the cost would fall on copper-nickel mining companies, which would be barred from staking claims or obtaining leases across the withdrawn area, and on the region's potential mining workforce, since development of copper, nickel, platinum, palladium, gold, and silver deposits there would not go forward. More broadly, the country would forgo that domestic source of metals used in batteries and electrical wiring, though the same deposits could still be developed elsewhere.

drawbacks.text: The withdrawal permanently forecloses development of copper, nickel, platinum-group metals, gold, and silver in the watershed, removing a potential domestic source of metals used in batteries, wiring, and clean-energy technology; those minerals would have to come from other domestic areas or imports.

Northeastern Minnesota has an economy and identity built on mining, and any new mine would have brought construction and operating jobs; the bill resolves that tradeoff one way, banking on the tourism findings while accepting that mining jobs in this specific watershed would not materialize.

Rather than letting the Forest Service complete a fresh environmental review of the withdrawal, the bill makes the withdrawal permanent by statute. The Forest Service had proposed a 20-year withdrawal in 2016, the Agriculture Department canceled it in 2018 about 20 months into a 24-month review, and this bill would sidestep that administrative process altogether.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stakes are lopsided in kind, not just size: acid mine drainage from a sulfide-ore operation in the watershed would be effectively impossible to undo, and the water flows straight through a million-acre wilderness and a national park into Canada. Against that, the cost is forgoing mineral development in one defined area while the bill explicitly keeps gravel, granite, iron ore, and taconite extraction available, and the bill's findings point to tourism growth that outweighs the mining jobs at stake. The main honest objection is process: a permanent congressional withdrawal settles by statute a question an ongoing environmental review could have answered, and it forfeits a domestic metals source at a time of growing demand.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its subcommittees for two years and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Betty McCollum introduced the bill on January 31, 2023, joined by 41 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
Cosponsorship grew to 48 House Democrats, all from McCollum's party; no Republican signed on.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources on January 31, 2023, and on February 21, 2023 was sent to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources and the Subcommittee on Federal Lands.
That is where the record ends: no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

The bill was Congress's answer to an unresolved dispute: the Forest Service had proposed a 20-year withdrawal of the same 234,328 acres in 2016, and the Department of Agriculture canceled that withdrawal application in 2018, about 20 months into a 24-month review, leaving the watershed open to mining under existing law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Copper-nickel mining interests came out ahead: with no vote ever held, the watershed remained open to mineral claims and leases under existing law, and no permanent statutory protection was enacted.

sides.party_line_note: There were no recorded votes, but the bill's 48 cosponsors were all Democrats and no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee never took it up.

industries.note: The bill would bar companies from staking claims or getting leases for copper, nickel, and platinum-group metals across 234,328 acres of the watershed. Its profit model depends on developing deposits whose acid runoff would fall on public water, wilderness, and the region's tourism economy.

Outfitters, lodges, and guide businesses depend on an unpolluted wilderness; the bill's findings project a withdrawal would add 1,500 to 4,600 jobs and $100 million to $900 million in income over 20 years compared with allowing the mining.

industries.industry: Iron ore, taconite, and aggregate producers
industries.note: The bill singles out sulfide-ore mining for the ban and expressly authorizes continued removal of sand, gravel, granite, iron ore, and taconite from the same area, so Minnesota's traditional iron mining keeps its access.
